opus-5.5.text:
I think math is special for a couple of reasons. The first is that it's one of the few domains where you can actually verify whether an answer is correct, and verify it perfectly. If you formalize a proof in a system like Lean, the checker either accepts it or it doesn't. There's no ambiguity and no human grader whose opinion might drift. That gives you a clean, scalable reward signal, and if you're doing reinforcement learning, that matters enormously. You can generate huge amounts of attempts, check them automatically, and learn from what works without being bottlenecked on human labeling.

The second reason is that math has a natural curriculum of difficulty that basically goes on forever. You start with grade-school arithmetic, move through competition problems, then undergraduate material, graduate-level theory, and finally open research problems that nobody has solved. So there's always a harder rung on the ladder, and the system can keep climbing without running out of meaningful challenges.

The third reason, and the one I find most exciting, is that math is really the distilled core of reasoning. To solve a hard problem you have to plan, break it into lemmas, try approaches, backtrack when something fails, and build on intermediate results over long chains of logic. Those are exactly the capabilities we want AI to have in general. If a system can do long-horizon, rigorous reasoning in math, a lot of that transfers to software verification, engineering, and science, anywhere correctness really matters.

And longer term, I think verified reasoning is how we get AI we can actually trust. Once outputs come with a proof attached, you don't have to take the model's word for it; you can check. Math is the training ground where we learn how to do that.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core problem with getting AI to do really hard reasoning is verification. If you want a model to work on something that takes a thousand steps, or ten thousand steps, you need to know whether it actually got it right, and you need to know that at scale, without a human checking every step. In most domains that's really hard. If a model writes a long legal argument or a research plan, who's going to grade it? You end up relying on human judgment, which is slow, expensive, and noisy, and it gets worse the harder the problem gets.

Math is the one domain where that problem basically goes away. If you write a proof in a formal language like Lean, the proof checker will tell you with certainty whether it's correct. There's no ambiguity, no partial credit, no reward hacking where the model learns to sound convincing instead of being right. That gives you a perfect, unlimited supply of reward signal. So you can let the model explore, generate lots of attempts, keep the ones that verify, and train on those, and the loop just keeps running.

The other piece is that math has a natural difficulty ladder. You can start with high school problems, move up to olympiad problems, then undergraduate, graduate, and eventually open research questions, and the verification works the same way the whole time. So it's not just that you can check the answers, it's that you can keep raising the bar essentially indefinitely, and the model never runs out of harder things to learn from.

And what we've found is that the capabilities you build this way aren't really about math specifically. Long chains of reasoning, planning, backtracking when something doesn't work, decomposing a problem into lemmas, these are general skills. Math is just the cleanest training ground for them, because it's the one place where the truth is machine-checkable.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics has two properties that make it particularly useful here. One is that you can pose problems across an enormous range of difficulty, from elementary arithmetic to questions that would take a professional mathematician years to solve. So as a model gets better, there’s always a harder problem to work on.

The other is that you can check whether an answer is correct. If you express a proof in a formal language, a proof checker can verify every step. That gives you a reliable feedback signal without needing a human to judge every response. A model can try different approaches, discover which ones work, and learn from those attempts.

And what makes that exciting is that solving harder math problems requires more than producing a plausible-looking answer. You have to choose useful intermediate steps, recognize when an approach is going nowhere, and sometimes build a new abstraction. Those are capabilities we’d like AI systems to develop more broadly. Mathematics gives us a setting where we can train and measure them precisely.

sol-6.1.text:
Mathematics gives you a very clean feedback signal. You can pose a problem that is extremely difficult to solve, but once you have a proof, you can check whether that proof is correct. If you work in a formal system, that checking can be done automatically, so you don’t need a human expert to judge every answer the model produces.

And there’s an enormous range of difficulty. You can start with elementary problems and move toward problems that require inventing useful intermediate results and combining ideas over many steps. That makes mathematics a rich environment for training reasoning: the model can explore different approaches, get reliable feedback, and gradually tackle harder problems.
